title: Small words, big attitude — the particles
goal: Hear and use the little particles that carry an Indonesian speaker's mood — *kan, kok, sih, deh, dong, lho, tuh, nih, ya, kali* — and know which ones are safe with friends only.
bekal: tell apart *kok* (surprise, reassurance), *kan* (you know, right?) and *lho* (hey, listen) in a conversation
soften or push a request with *deh*, *dong*, *ya* and point at news with *nih* and *tuh*
read a casual chat message full of particles and answer in the same tone

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Kabar dari warung
dialogs.intro: A hot afternoon in June. Sarah is helping Bu Ratna fold sheets in the homestay's back room when Bu Ratna lowers her voice. The subject: Yoga, and Bu Ratna's niece Wulan, who runs the little warung by the village square.

lines.speaker: Ratna:
lines.text: Mbak Sarah, sini deh. Ada kabar, nih.
lines.id: Sarah, come here a sec. I've got some news.
lines.literal: miss Sarah, here [deh]. exist news, [nih].

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Kabar apa sih, Bu? Kok pakai bisik-bisik segala?
lines.id: What news? Why all the whispering?
lines.literal: news what [sih], Madam? [kok] use whisper-whisper all?

lines.speaker: Ratna:
lines.text: Yoga, lho. Tiap sore dia mampir ke warung Wulan.
lines.id: It's Yoga, listen. Every afternoon he drops in at Wulan's warung.
lines.literal: Yoga, [lho]. every afternoon he drop-by to stall Wulan.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Wulan keponakan Ibu, kan? Ya wajar dong, dia beli es teh.
lines.id: Wulan's your niece, isn't she? Well, that's normal, he buys iced tea.
lines.literal: Wulan niece Madam, [kan]? [ya] normal [dong], he buy ice tea.

lines.speaker: Ratna:
lines.text: Beli es teh kok tiap hari? Dua jam lagi.
lines.id: Iced tea every single day? For two hours?
lines.literal: buy ice tea [kok] every day? two hour more.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Hmm, iya juga, ya. Kemarin dia pinjam motor saya, katanya mau ke Muntilan.
lines.id: Hmm, you've got a point. Yesterday he borrowed my motorbike, said he was going to Muntilan.
lines.literal: hmm, yes also, [ya]. yesterday he borrow motorbike my, said-it want to Muntilan.

lines.speaker: Ratna:
lines.text: Nah, tuh! Wulan kemarin juga ke Muntilan. Kebetulan, kali?
lines.id: There you go! Wulan went to Muntilan yesterday too. Pure coincidence, I'm sure.
lines.literal: [nah], [tuh]! Wulan yesterday also to Muntilan. coincidence, [kali]?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Ibu ini kayak detektif, ya. Jangan-jangan Ibu yang atur.
lines.id: You're like a detective. I bet you set it all up.
lines.literal: Madam this like detective, [ya]. don't-don't Madam who arrange.

lines.speaker: Ratna:
lines.text: Ih, bukan saya! Tapi saya sih setuju saja. Anaknya sopan, kok.
lines.id: Oh, not me! But I'm all for it, personally. He's a polite boy, really.
lines.literal: [ih], not me! but I [sih] agree only. child-the polite, [kok].

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Terus Wulannya gimana? Suka juga?
lines.id: And what about Wulan? Does she like him too?
lines.literal: then Wulan-the how? like also?

lines.speaker: Ratna:
lines.text: Ya mana saya tahu. Coba Mbak tanya Yoga, dong. Mbak kan bosnya.
lines.id: How should I know? You ask Yoga, go on. You're his boss, after all.
lines.literal: [ya] where I know. try miss ask Yoga, [dong]. miss [kan] boss-his.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Lho, kok saya? Nggak, ah. Itu urusan anak muda.
lines.id: Hang on, why me? No way. That's young people's business.
lines.literal: [lho], [kok] me? no, [ah]. that business child young.

lines.speaker: Ratna:
lines.text: Ayo dong, Mbak. Sedikit saja. Nanti saya bikinkan getuk, deh.
lines.id: Oh, come on. Just a little. I'll make you some getuk, how about that.
lines.literal: come-on [dong], miss. little only. later I make-for getuk, [deh].

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Ya sudah, deh. Tapi kalau dia marah, Ibu yang tanggung, lho.
lines.id: Oh, all right then. But if he gets cross, it's on you, mind.
lines.literal: [ya] already, [deh]. but if he angry, Madam who bear, [lho].

notes: **Sini deh / Ya sudah, deh.** *Deh* has two faces. After an invitation or offer it softens and coaxes: *Coba deh* (go on, try it), *Nanti saya bikinkan getuk, deh* (I'll make you getuk, how's that). After agreement it signals giving in: *Ya sudah, deh* — “oh, all right then”.

**Nih and tuh** are short for *ini* and *itu* and literally point: *nih* at something close or new (*Ada kabar, nih* — “got some news here”), *tuh* at something over there or already proven (*Nah, tuh!* — “see, there you go!”). *Nih* is also what you say handing something over: *Nih, kuncinya.*

**Kok** marks surprise that something is the way it is: *Kok bisik-bisik?* (why are you whispering, of all things?), *Beli es teh kok tiap hari?* At the end of a statement it does the opposite and reassures: *Anaknya sopan, kok* — “he's polite, honestly”.

**Kan** asks for agreement you already expect: *Wulan keponakan Ibu, kan?* (she's your niece, isn't she?). Inside a sentence it means “after all, as you know”: *Mbak kan bosnya* — “you're the boss, after all”. It comes from *bukan*.

**Kali** at the end of a sentence is Jakarta-style “maybe, I suppose”, from *barangkali*. Said with a raised eyebrow, as Bu Ratna does, it becomes irony: *Kebetulan, kali?* — “just a coincidence, I'm sure”. ⚠️ Keep it for friends; it sounds cheeky to superiors.

**Jangan-jangan** — “I bet, don't tell me” — introduces a suspicion: *Jangan-jangan dia lupa* (I bet he's forgotten). **Wulannya** — *-nya* on a name means “the Wulan we're discussing”: *Wulannya gimana?* is completely natural speech. *Bikinkan* is the everyday form of *buatkan* (make for someone).

grammars.title: Particles of feeling: kok, kan, lho, sih, dong
body: These five carry emotion rather than information. Remove them and the sentence still means the same, but it loses its tone of voice.

head: Particle
Core feeling
Example
English feel
rows: surprise, “how come?”; reassurance at the end
How come it's so expensive? / It's good, really.
“hey, listen, did you know”; mild alarm
*Lho, kamu di sini? / Awas, panas, lho.*
Oh, you're here? / Careful, it's hot, mind.
What's up, then? / I'm fine with it, personally.
Help me, come on! / Well, of course.

after: *Lho* and *kok* often team up at the start: *Lho, kok saya?* — “hang on, why me?”. Together they are pure surprise.
⚠️ *Dong* pushes. Among friends it is warm; to a boss or a stranger it can sound like an order. *Tolong… ya* is the polite way to ask.

grammars.title: Pointing and softening: nih, tuh, deh, ya, kali
body: The second group mostly adjusts position and pressure: pointing at something, easing a request, or hedging a claim.

head: Particle
Job
Example
English feel
rows: Go on, try it. / OK then.

after: *Ya* is the one particle that is polite everywhere, including with the Bupati's staff: *Mohon ditunggu, ya, Pak.* If you only ever use one particle, use this one.
*Tuh, kan!* — “see, what did I say!” — is one of the most satisfying phrases in the language, and you will hear it whenever a prediction comes true.

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Chat dengan Yoga
dialogs.intro: That evening Sarah messages Yoga about tomorrow's briefing. Chat Indonesian is even more particle-heavy than speech, and Yoga types exactly the way he talks.

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Mbak, besok briefing jam delapan, kan? Aku bawa proyektor, ya.
lines.id: Sarah, tomorrow's briefing is at eight, right? I'll bring the projector.
lines.literal: miss, tomorrow briefing hour eight, [kan]? I bring projector, [ya].

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Iya. Eh, kemarin ke Muntilan ngapain, sih?
lines.id: Yes. Oh, by the way, what were you doing in Muntilan yesterday?
lines.literal: yes. [eh], yesterday to Muntilan do-what, [sih]?

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Lho, kok Mbak tahu? Pasti Bu Ratna, nih.
lines.id: Hang on, how do you know? This has got Bu Ratna written all over it.
lines.literal: [lho], [kok] miss know? surely Mrs Ratna, [nih].

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Hehe. Nggak usah panik, dong. Aku cuma nanya.
lines.id: Hehe. No need to panic. I'm only asking.
lines.literal: hehe. not need panic, [dong]. I only ask.

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Aku nganter Wulan beli bahan kue doang. Serius, Mbak.
lines.id: I just took Wulan to buy baking stuff, that's all. Seriously.
lines.literal: I accompany Wulan buy ingredient cake only. serious, miss.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Iya, iya, percaya kok. Tapi motornya balikin dengan bensin penuh, ya.
lines.id: Yes, yes, I believe you. But bring the bike back with a full tank, OK?
lines.literal: yes, yes, believe [kok]. but motorbike-the return-it with petrol full, [ya].

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Siap! Udah kuisi tadi pagi. Jangan bilang siapa-siapa, ya, Mbak.
lines.id: Will do! I filled it up this morning. Don't tell anyone, OK?
lines.literal: ready! already I-fill earlier morning. don't say who-who, [ya], miss.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Tenang aja. Tapi Bu Ratna udah tahu duluan, lho.
lines.id: Relax. But Bu Ratna knew before I did, you know.
lines.literal: calm just. but Mrs Ratna already know first, [lho].

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Yah, ketahuan deh. Ya udah, sekalian aja aku ajak Wulan ke festival.
lines.id: Oh well, busted. Fine then, I might as well ask Wulan to the festival.
lines.literal: [yah], found-out [deh]. [ya] already, at-once just I invite Wulan to festival.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Nah, gitu dong! Semangat, Yoga.
lines.id: That's more like it! Go for it, Yoga.
lines.literal: [nah], like-that [dong]! spirit, Yoga.

notes: **Sarah switches to aku.** With Yoga, a young intern in a private chat, Sarah drops *saya* for *aku* — a small sign of friendliness. In the office in front of Pak Harun she will be back to *saya*. Choosing the pronoun is choosing the distance.

**Ngapain** — “doing what?” — is built from *apa* with Jakarta *nge-…-in* (standard: *sedang apa*, *melakukan apa*), and one of the most useful casual words there is: *Lagi ngapain?* (what are you up to?). Here *sih* makes the question curious rather than accusing.
**Doang** is Jakarta-style “only, just”, placed at the end: *beli bahan kue doang* = *hanya membeli bahan kue*. It is very common among young people all over Java and in chat.

**Udah kuisi** — the “thing + person + verb” passive again, with *aku* shortened to *ku-* and written joined: *kuisi* (I filled), *kubeli*, *kubaca*. It is casual but perfectly correct in writing too.
**Ketahuan** — “found out, caught”. Like *kehujanan*, it is a *ke-an* word for something that happens to you against your will. *Yah… ketahuan deh* is the classic phrase of the busted.

**Gitu dong!** — “that's the way!” — is *dong* at its most positive: approval of something that should obviously be done. *Semangat!* (spirit!) is the all-purpose Indonesian “go for it, good luck, you can do it”.

grammars.title: One sentence, six moods
body: The clearest way to hear what particles do is to hang them one by one on the same short sentence. Here is *Dia datang* (“he's coming”).

head: Indonesian
Mood
English feel
rows: Why on earth has he come?

after: Position matters: *kok* usually goes first or right before the surprising part, *kan*, *kok* (reassuring), *lho*, *deh* and *kali* go last, and *sih* sits right after the word it softens.
Particles are unstressed and short, but they shape the tune of the whole sentence. *Kok mahal?* rises sharply on *mahal*; *Enak, kok* falls gently and warmly. Copy the melody when you copy the words.
Chat spelling varies: *lho* is also written *loh*, and *kok* appears as *koq* in older messages. They are the same particles.

sections.title: Particle combinations you will hear every day

blocks.text: Particles love company. These pairs and phrases are fixed, and each one is worth learning as a single chunk with its own tune.

head: Phrase
English feel
When
rows: Why would you do that? / That's not fair!

blocks.text: Most of these come from Jakarta speech but are understood everywhere. In Central Java you will also hear *to* (*Iya, to?* — “isn't it?”) and *je* (*Aku ra ngerti, je* — “I just don't know”), which do similar jobs.

blocks.title: How to practise particles
items: Watch an Indonesian sitcom or vlog and count the particles in one minute. Twenty is not unusual.
Pick one particle a week. Use *kok* for reassurance this week (*Nggak apa-apa, kok*), *deh* for offers next week (*Aku traktir, deh*).
Listen for how your friends answer *Makasih, ya*: often *Sama-sama, kok* or *Santai aja*. The particle makes the answer warm.

blocks.text: Particles belong to speech and chat, and a few of them can make you sound rude to the wrong person. Use this as a rough guide.

blocks.title: Particles in writing
items: Emails and letters to officials: no particles at all. A chat message to a colleague: *ya* and *kok* are fine.

*-lah* is the one particle that belongs to formal writing too: *Silakan duduklah* is old-fashioned, but *Inilah hasilnya* (this, then, is the result) is everyday written style. Unit 17 comes back to it.
If you are unsure how a particle sounds, leave it out. A sentence without particles is only neutral; the wrong particle is a tone of voice you did not mean.

blocks.text: Cover the Indonesian column, read the English, and rebuild each sentence from memory.

head: English
Indonesian
rows: Ladies and gentlemen, as it is nine o'clock, I declare this meeting open.
*Bapak-Ibu sekalian, karena sudah pukul sembilan, rapat ini saya buka.*
Three, if possible. Javanese too, so that visitors learn a bit as well.
*Kalau bisa tiga, Bu. Bahasa Jawa juga, biar tamu ikut belajar.*
Agreed. The homestay group is ready to chip in to cover the shortfall.
*Setuju, Pak. Kelompok homestay siap urunan untuk kekurangannya.*
Sarah, the minutes are done. Could you check them? I was half asleep when I wrote them, mind you.
*Mbak, notulennya udah jadi. Tolong dicek, ya. Aku nulisnya sambil ngantuk, sih.*
Also, don't mix the decisions in with the discussion. Put them under a separate point.
*Terus, keputusan jangan dicampur dengan diskusi. Tulis di poin tersendiri.*
